meta.title: Theme setup
meta.description: One-time theme setup for beUI components: install the shadcn token layer, or paste the beUI theme CSS into your globals.css.
meta.ogDescription: One-time theme setup for beUI components: shadcn tokens or the beUI theme CSS.

theme.title: Theme setup
theme.intro: beUI components style themselves with shadcn semantic tokens (bg-primary, text-muted-foreground, border, ring). Set those tokens up once and every component works. Two ways:

option1.title: Option 1 — shadcn init (recommended)
option1.body: If your project uses shadcn, you already have these tokens. Otherwise run init once; it writes the token layer into your CSS.

option2.title: Option 2 — paste the theme CSS
option2.body: Not using shadcn? Paste this into your globals.css directly below @import "tailwindcss";. It defines the tokens, motion animations and surface utilities the components use. Requires Tailwind CSS v4.

meta.title: AI Agents
meta.description: Install the beUI agent skill, connect the MCP server, or use the agent-friendly endpoints (llms.txt, JSON registry, raw source) to consume components programmatically.

header.title: For AI agents
header.intro: beUI exposes a static, agent-friendly surface. Install the beUI skill, connect the MCP server below, or hit the raw endpoints directly. Coding agents (Claude, Codex, Cursor, Amp) can list components, fetch source with all deps, and drop files into the user's project.

agentSkill.title: Agent skill
agentSkill.body: The skill teaches coding agents to fetch the live registry first, pick the closest items[].name install slug, inspect it with shadcn, then install and compose from the generated source. Use it when you want agents to choose existing beUI components instead of inventing custom motion widgets.

mcpServer.title: MCP server
mcpServer.body: The fastest path: connect the beUI MCP server and your agent can list, search and install components directly. Hosted at {url}.
mcpServer.manual: Any other client: add it manually to your MCP config.
mcpServer.toolsWithNative: Tools: list_components, search_components, get_component, get_install_command. For React Native apps, list_native_components and get_native_component return beUI Native components with every file to copy.

shadcnItem.label: shadcn item
shadcnItem.desc: Install item with inline file content and shadcn semantic color classes.

rawSource.label: Raw source
rawSource.desc: Plain text .tsx ready to drop in.

agentFlow.title: Agent flow
agentFlow.body: Four calls, then install. Components are self-contained and own their files.

shadcnFlow.title: shadcn flow
shadcnFlow.body: The shadcn item installs source files and package dependencies. Components use shadcn semantic color utilities directly, so they inherit the target app's theme without beUI-specific color variables.

entryShape.title: Entry shape
entryShape.body: Internal helpers (e.g. @/lib/utils) ship inline as type: util so the agent does not have to chase imports.

generativeUi.title: Generative UI
generativeUi.body: Want the model to compose these components into a live interface? Follow the <link>OpenUI integration guide</link> to register a custom component library, generate its system prompt, and render interactive OpenUI Lang as it streams.

meta.title: OpenUI integration guide
meta.description: Build an OpenUI React integration with beUI. Register animated components, generate the system prompt, stream OpenUI Lang, and render interactive UI.

header.title: Use beUI with OpenUI
header.intro: OpenUI is a generative UI framework: instead of returning markdown, the model emits an abstract UI tree (OpenUI Lang) and a React runtime maps every node to a component you register. This OpenUI React integration turns beUI into a custom OpenUI component library, so each generated response uses real, animated components—and only the components you allow.

install.title: Install
install.body: You need OpenUI's React runtime and the beUI components you want to expose. Pull beUI source with the shadcn registry (see the <link>AI Agents</link> guide for other install paths).
install.scaffold: Scaffolding from scratch? Run {command} for a working streaming app, then swap its default library for the beUI one below.

registerComponents.title: Register components
registerComponents.body: defineComponent maps one OpenUI Lang node to a beUI component. The Zod props schema validates the model's output as it streams, the description is injected into the system prompt so the model learns each component's intent, and useTriggerAction keeps rendered controls interactive. Describe a container's children as a union of the registered .ref schemas so nesting is both validated and advertised to the model.

assembleLibrary.title: Assemble the library
assembleLibrary.body: createLibrary collects the definitions, names the root node, and organises the prompt into componentGroups with notes that steer how the model reaches for each one.

generatePrompt.title: Generate the prompt
generatePrompt.body: The client renders OpenUI Lang, but the model has to produce it. In the CLI, call {command} to build the library spec. The backend combines its component signatures, descriptions, and nesting constraints with the OpenUI Lang grammar, then streams the model's reply back to the browser.
generatePrompt.note: Run that command when the library changes. It serializes the library to JSON at build time, and the route imports that generated file through the same @/lib/generated path, so the server bundle never imports your client components.

renderStream.title: Render the stream
renderStream.body: Pass the library to {renderer} on the client. It parses the OpenUI Lang your server streams and paints beUI components progressively as tokens arrive. Wire onAction to send a pressed button's message back to the model and continue the loop.

whyBeui.title: Why beUI fits
whyBeui.body: beUI components own their files and ship through the registry, so there's no runtime to bolt on — the library above is the integration. They use semantic controls and shadcn tokens, so model-generated UIs inherit the host app's theme without extra wiring.

meta.title: Motion Guides
meta.description: Practical motion guidance for React interfaces: when to animate, which beUI token to use, timing ranges, reduced motion, and copy-ready patterns.
meta.ogDescription: Practical guidance for purposeful animation, timing, easing, springs, and accessible motion in React interfaces.

header.title: Motion that explains, not distracts
header.intro: A practical guide to deciding when something should move, choosing the right token, and shipping motion that stays fast, coherent, and accessible.

decisionFramework.title: Four questions before motion
decisionFramework.description: The best animation decision is often made before touching a duration or spring value.

motionTokens.title: Use one language everywhere
motionTokens.description: beUI keeps deliberate motion in shared tokens. Choose by purpose so components feel related without moving identically.

timing.title: Fast enough to feel immediate
timing.description: Duration depends on size, distance, and frequency. These ranges are starting points, not targets to hit mechanically.

recipes.title: Patterns you can copy
recipes.description: Each recipe connects a purpose to a production token, a reduced-motion state, and a concrete failure mode.

accessibility.title: Reduced motion is a designed state
accessibility.description: Do not remove every transition. Keep feedback that helps comprehension and remove movement that can cause discomfort.

frequency.title: Check frequency
frequency.body: Repeated actions should feel nearly instant. Save expressive motion for moments users see occasionally.
frequency.note: 100× a day: no choreography. Rare moments: more delight is allowed.

purpose.title: Name the purpose
purpose.body: Motion should explain space, confirm input, show state, or soften a change. Decoration alone is not enough.
purpose.note: If you cannot explain why it moves, remove the movement.

physics.title: Choose the physics
physics.body: Use ease-out for entrances, ease-in-out for movement, linear for progress, and springs for gestures.
physics.note: The curve should match what the object is doing, not personal taste.

fallback.title: Design the fallback
fallback.body: Reduced motion keeps useful opacity and color feedback while removing travel, scale, and parallax.
fallback.note: Accessibility is a motion state, not an afterthought.

timing.note: Under 300ms is the default for interface motion. Longer motion belongs to explanatory demos, deliberate gestures, and large spatial changes.

easing.title: Compare the curves
easing.subtitle: Same distance and duration. Different jobs.
easing.easeOut: Entrances and exits respond immediately, then settle quietly.
easing.easeInOut: Objects already on screen accelerate and decelerate naturally.
easing.springPress: Fast, weighted feedback for buttons and other pressable surfaces.
easing.springLayout: Shared surfaces and indicators that need continuous spatial movement.

press.title: Press feedback
press.description: A press should acknowledge input before the action finishes. Keep the scale small and the response immediate.
press.purpose: Confirms that the interface heard the user.
press.avoid: Large scale changes, slow rebounds, or a spring on every child.

icon.title: Semantic icon motion
icon.description: Let the icon imitate its real action. A bell swings from its hinge; a download arrow drops toward its tray.
icon.purpose: Reinforces what the action does without adding another label.
icon.avoid: The same generic bounce on every icon, or motion on touch hover.

reveal.title: Content reveal
reveal.description: Reveal one meaningful surface with a short lift and restrained blur. The motion should finish before it becomes the focus.
reveal.purpose: Prevents new content from appearing as a jarring visual cut.
reveal.avoid: Half-second UI entrances or a long stagger across every small child.

layout.title: Layout continuity
layout.description: Keep the same surface visible while its footprint changes. Move the shape first, then introduce its label.
layout.purpose: Preserves object identity while a compact control expands.
layout.avoid: Direct width tweens or text appearing before the surface makes room.

swap.title: Content swap
swap.description: For small view changes, let the old content leave faster than the new content arrives. Keep travel to a few pixels.
swap.purpose: Clarifies that content changed while the surrounding context stayed put.
swap.avoid: Large page-like transitions for tabs, filters, or frequently changed views.

accessibility.title: Keep meaning. Remove travel.
accessibility.body: Preserve opacity, color, and instant state changes. Drop parallax, large transforms, repeated scale, and spring overshoot.

meta.title: Playground
meta.description: Tweak spring, tween and stagger properties, watch them play, and copy the motion code. Built on beUI's motion tokens.

header.title: Playground
header.body: Learn motion by playing. Tweak a property, watch it run, read what the code is doing line by line, then copy it.

spring.label: Spring
spring.blurb: Physics-based motion. Stiffness pulls toward the target, damping resists, mass adds weight. Lower damping overshoots.

stiffness.label: Stiffness
stiffness.hint: Pull toward the target. Higher = faster, snappier.

damping.label: Damping
damping.hint: Resistance / friction. Lower = more bounce and overshoot.

mass.label: Mass
mass.hint: Weight of the object. Heavier = slower, more sluggish.

explain.type: No duration here. Instead of taking a fixed time, the box is pulled to the target like it's on a real spring. The three numbers below decide how that feels.
explain.stiffness: How hard the spring pulls. {value} is {level, select, soft {soft, so it moves slowly} medium {medium} other {strong, so it snaps fast}}. Higher = faster, more urgent.
explain.damping: Friction that slows the spring down. {level, select, low {{value} is low, so the box overshoots the target and bounces before settling.} medium {{value} gives a little overshoot, then settles.} other {{value} is high, so it eases in with no bounce.}}
explain.mass: The box's weight. {level, select, light {{value} is light, so it reacts quickly.} heavy {{value} is heavy, so it feels sluggish and slow to start.} other {{value} is medium weight.}} Heavier = slower, more inertia.

tween.label: Tween / Ease
tween.blurb: Time-based motion. Duration sets how long; the cubic-bezier curve sets the pacing. Drag the handles to shape it.

duration.label: Duration
duration.hint: How long the animation takes, start to finish.

curve.label: Easing curve
curve.hint: Pacing over time. Drag the handles — steep = fast, flat = slow.

curves.linear: Constant speed the whole way. Mechanical, no acceleration.
curves.easeIn: Starts slow, speeds up into the end. Good for things leaving.
curves.easeOut: Starts fast, slows into the end. Good for things arriving.
curves.easeInOut: Slow start and finish, fast through the middle. Smooth and natural.
curves.custom: Your own pacing. Steeper parts of the curve move faster.

explain.duration: A fixed time, in seconds. The whole move always takes {value}s, no matter the distance. (Springs don't have this — tweens do.)
explain.ease: The easing curve, written as a cubic-bezier. The four numbers are two control handles (x1, y1, x2, y2) that bend how speed changes over time. You rarely type these by hand — drag the curve handles instead.
explain.curve: This curve reads as "{title}": {text} The dots in the preview are the box's position at equal time slices, so spacing shows speed.

stagger.label: Stagger
stagger.blurb: Children animate in sequence. Stagger sets the gap between each; delay holds the whole group before it starts.

stagger.label: Stagger
stagger.hint: Gap between each child starting. Higher = more of a wave.

delayChildren.label: Delay
delayChildren.hint: Pause before the whole group begins.

explain.variants: Two named states. "hidden" is the start (invisible, small, nudged down), "show" is the end. Every child animates from hidden to show — you describe states, not steps.
explain.staggerChildren: The gap between each child starting, in seconds. They don't all fire at once — child 2 waits {value}s after child 1, and so on, making the wave.
explain.delayChildren: How long the whole group waits before the first child starts. {immediate, select, yes {0 = starts immediately.} other {Here, {value}s of dead time up front.}}
explain.summary: With {count} children at {stagger}s apart{delayed, select, yes { after a {delay}s delay} other {}}, the last one begins {last}s in. {direction, select, reverse {Reverse means the last child fires first.} other {Forward fires them first-to-last.}}

keyframes.label: Keyframes
keyframes.blurb: A property steps through a list of values in order, evenly spaced across the duration. Edit the list to change where it goes.

property.label: Property
property.hint: Which property the keyframes drive. Switching it resets the values.

frames.label: Keyframe values
frames.hint: Each slider is a checkpoint the box passes through, in order. Drag one, or add/remove checkpoints.

duration.label: Duration
duration.hint: Time for one pass through all the values.

repeat.label: Repeat
repeat.hint: Once, loop from the start, or mirror back and forth.

describe.scale: {percent}% size{trend, select, bigger {, bigger} smaller {, smaller} other {, normal}}
describe.opacity: {percent}% visible{state, select, invisible {, invisible} solid {, solid} other {}}
describe.x: {value}px {side, select, right {right of} left {left of} other {at}} start

read.scale: {value} ({percent}% size{trend, select, bigger {, bigger} smaller {, smaller} other {, normal}})

explain.sequence: This array is a list of values the box passes through, in order: {sequence}. It's not "from A to B" — it hits every value as a checkpoint.
explain.spacing: The values are spaced evenly across the duration. {count} values over {duration}s means each leg takes about {leg}s. Add or remove values to change the path.
explain.loop: Loop: when it reaches the last value it jumps back to the first and runs again — so it can snap at the seam.
explain.mirror: Mirror: it plays forward, then backward, then forward — smooth, no snap, like a pulse.
explain.once: Once: it runs a single time and stops on the last value.

gestures.label: Gestures
gestures.blurb: Motion responds to pointer input. whileHover and whileTap animate to a state during the gesture; drag makes an element throwable.

hover.label: Hover scale
hover.hint: Size while the pointer is over it.

tap.label: Tap scale
tap.hint: Size while pressed. Under 1 = a press-in.

drag.label: Drag
drag.hint: Constrain dragging to an axis, free, or off.

explain.hover: While the pointer is over the box, animate to {value}× size ({percent}%). It springs back to normal when the pointer leaves — no state or handlers needed.
explain.tap: While it's being pressed, go to {value}× size. {pressIn, select, yes {Under 1 = a press-in, the tactile feel of a real button.} other {At 1 it stays put on press.}}
explain.drag: Makes the box draggable{mode, select, free { in any direction} other { on the {mode}-axis only}}. dragConstraints keeps it inside its parent, and it springs back if thrown past the edge.

layout.label: Layout
layout.blurb: A shared layoutId morphs one element into another when which one is mounted changes, so an indicator glides between positions instead of jumping.

feel.label: Feel
feel.hint: The transition the pill travels with.

explain.layoutId: The key idea. Only one pill is rendered — under the active tab. When you click another tab, React unmounts it here and mounts it there, but the shared layoutId tells Motion they're the same element, so it animates between the two positions instead of popping.
explain.conditional: The pill only exists inside the active tab. You don't compute any positions or offsets yourself — Motion measures the old and new spots and tweens the gap automatically.
explain.transition: Controls how the pill travels. {feel, select, Slow {A timed tween — same duration every move.} Snappy {A spring — stiff, so it snaps over quickly.} other {A spring — softer, so it glides.}}

scroll.label: Scroll
scroll.blurb: Scroll-linked motion ties a value to scroll position. useScroll reports 0→1 progress; useTransform maps that range onto a transform.

effect.label: Effect
effect.hint: What the box does as the panel scrolls.

explain.useScroll: Watches how far the panel is scrolled and gives back scrollYProgress: a number from 0 (scrolled to top) to 1 (scrolled to bottom). It updates on every scroll frame.
explain.useTransform: Remaps that 0→1 progress onto a real value range. As progress goes 0→1, {prop} goes {range} — so at the top it's {start}, at the bottom {end}.
explain.style: The mapped value is a live motion value wired straight into the box's style, so it tracks your scroll exactly — scroll up and it runs in reverse.

meta.title: Set up beUI Native in your React Native app
meta.description: One-time setup for beUI Native: install Reanimated, Gesture Handler and Uniwind, configure Metro, add the theme tokens, then copy in any component.

header.title: Set up beUI Native
header.intro: beUI Native components are plain source you copy into your app, like the web components. Do the setup below once per app. After that, adding a component is copying its files from its page. It works in Expo and in bare React Native.

requirements.title: Requirements
requirements.body: The components are built and tested against these versions.

install.title: 1. Install the libraries
install.body: In an Expo app, expo install picks the versions that match your SDK. Uniwind and Tailwind come from npm.
install.babelNote: Expo's Babel preset already includes the Worklets plugin that Reanimated 4 needs. In a bare React Native app, add it to babel.config.js yourself:

uniwind.title: 2. Set up Uniwind
uniwind.body: Components are styled with Tailwind class names through Uniwind. Create global.css in the project root. It loads Tailwind, Uniwind and the beUI theme you add in the next step.
uniwind.metro: Then point Metro at it. withUniwindConfig must be the outermost wrapper if you use other Metro wrappers, and cssEntryFile must be a relative path.
uniwind.bareNote: In a bare React Native app, the default config comes from @react-native/metro-config instead:
uniwind.typesNote: Uniwind writes the class name types to dtsFile when Metro starts, so start it once before checking types. If TypeScript then can't find the global.css import, declare CSS files:

theme.title: 3. Add the theme tokens
theme.body: Components use semantic colors like bg-primary and text-muted, defined for light and dark mode, so they follow the system appearance. Save this file as {path}, the path global.css imports, and change the values to match your brand.

root.title: 4. Wrap your app
root.body: Import global.css from your root component, not from the file that registers the app, or every style change reloads the whole app. Wrap the app in GestureHandlerRootView so swipeable and draggable components can receive gestures. With Expo Router, both go in the root layout:
root.bareNote: In a bare app, do the same in App.tsx. For forms, also wrap the app in KeyboardProvider from react-native-keyboard-controller to keep focused fields above the keyboard.

addComponent.title: 5. Add a component
addComponent.cli: Run the beUI Native CLI from your app's root. It copies the component and the shared files it needs into src/ and installs any libraries you don't have yet.
addComponent.manual: To copy files by hand instead, open the component from the <link>React Native components</link> and use its Manual steps. Either way, keep the folder layout, since components import shared files by relative path. Tabs ends up like this:
addComponent.usage: Then use it like any other component:
addComponent.sourceNote: Tailwind finds class names in files under the folder that holds global.css. If it lives somewhere else, like app/, add an @source for the components:

tryFirst.title: Try before you copy
tryFirst.body: Every React Native component page has a recording in light and dark, so you can see the motion first. Coding agents can fetch any component with its install commands and files from {url}, or through the beUI MCP server. See the Agent Guide.
tryFirst.note: Every component follows the system Reduce Motion setting and takes a disableAnimation prop. The source is on GitHub.
